subject: mathematics_2a
question_text: A random variable X has the range {1, 2, 3, …}. If P(X = k) = cᵏ/k! for k = 1, 2, 3, …, then find c and P(0 < X < 3).

mark_split.label: Sum the series and find c

recall_prompt: Say how you would find c and P(0 < X < 3) when P(X = k) = cᵏ/k! — what series the probabilities make, which standard series it is, and which terms the probability needs.
insider_note: Σ P(X = k) = 1 written as the series c/1! + c²/2! + … is where the first marks sit; the series is eᶜ with its leading 1 missing, so add 1 to BOTH sides to get eᶜ = 2 — and the final answer stays as logₑ 2, never a decimal.

steps.label: Write ΣP = 1 as a series
steps.margin_note: First two marks. X has infinitely many values, so ΣP(X = k) = 1 is an infinite series: c/1! + c²/2! + c³/3! + … = 1. Write the general term first and then the series with at least three terms and the dots.

recall.must_convey: That ΣP(X = k) = 1 becomes the infinite series c/1! + c²/2! + c³/3! + … = 1.
accept: the probabilities add to one so c by one factorial plus c squared by two factorial plus c cubed by three factorial and so on equals one
sum of P equals one gives an infinite series in c starting from k equals one
write c over one factorial plus c square over two factorial plus dot dot dot equal to one
anni probabilities kalipithe one, c by one factorial plus c square by two factorial plus so on equals one
set the infinite sum of c to the k over k factorial equal to one

steps.why: With an infinite range the condition ΣP = 1 is a series, and the whole question is recognising which series. Writing enough terms to see the pattern is what earns these marks.
common_mistakes: Starting the series at k = 0 with a term 1 — the range starts at 1.
Writing c/1! + c/2! + c/3! without the powers of c.
Stopping after one or two terms so the pattern cannot be seen.

steps.label: Sum the series and find c
steps.margin_note: Three marks — the main idea. The series is the exponential series with its first term 1 missing: 1 + x/1! + x²/2! + x³/3! + … = eˣ. Add 1 to both sides, so the left side becomes eᶜ and the right side 2. Then c = logₑ 2.
lines: We know 1 + x/1! + x²/2! + x³/3! + … = eˣ

recall.must_convey: That adding 1 turns the left side into the exponential series eᶜ, so eᶜ = 2 and c = logₑ 2.
accept: add one to both sides, the left side is the exponential series e to the c, so e to the c is two and c is log e of two
the series is e to the x without the first term, so e to the c minus one equals one and c equals natural log two
recognise the exponential series, e to the c equals two, c is log two to the base e
one add cheste e power c vastundi, e power c equals two, c equals log e two
c is the natural logarithm of two

steps.why: The exponential series is the one standard series whose terms are xᵏ/k!, and the missing first term is the reason for adding 1 to both sides. Once eᶜ = 2 is written, c is a single logarithm.
common_mistakes: Writing eᶜ = 1 by forgetting to add 1 to the right side as well.
Trying to sum the series as a geometric series.

steps.label: Find P(0 < X < 3)
steps.margin_note: Last two marks. 0 < X < 3 on the range {1, 2, 3, …} means X = 1 or 2. Add the two terms c/1! + c²/2! = c + c²/2 and put c = logₑ 2. The answer stays in logarithms; there is no simpler form.

recall.must_convey: That P(0 < X < 3) = P(X = 1) + P(X = 2) = c + c²/2 = logₑ 2 + (logₑ 2)²/2.
accept: P of zero less than X less than three is P of one plus P of two which is c plus c squared by two with c equal to log e two

steps.why: The event keeps the values 1 and 2 of the range, and the probability is the sum of those two terms of the series — the same terms already written in the first step.
common_mistakes: Including X = 0, which is not in the range.
Writing c²/2! as c², forgetting the 2 in the denominator.
Replacing logₑ 2 by 0.693 without being asked — keep the exact form.
